posts.title: Structured Decoding: Making an LLM Incapable of Invalid Output
posts.subtitle: Instead of asking nicely for JSON and hoping, mask out every token that would break the schema.
posts.summary: Structured (constrained) decoding compiles a target schema — JSON Schema, a regex, a context-free grammar — into a state machine over tokens, then masks the model's logits at every decode step so only schema-valid tokens can be sampled. The output is syntactically guaranteed to match, with no retry loop and no fine-tuning required — though it only constrains shape, not truth.

bullets: Works on any open-weight model, zero fine-tuning
Guarantees syntax, not semantics
Used under the hood by vLLM, llama.cpp grammars, Outlines, and most agent tool-calling stacks
slides.body: A prompt like 'reply only with JSON' is a request the model can still ignore — structured decoding makes ignoring it physically impossible.
slides.title: Don't Ask for Valid JSON. Enforce It.

bullets: A parser crash on malformed output breaks the whole downstream pipeline
Retry-until-valid loops add latency and cost, and still aren't guaranteed to succeed
In an agent loop, one bad tool-call payload can derail the entire run
slides.body: Prompting alone leaves the model free to add a stray sentence before the brace, invent a field that isn't in your schema, or drop a closing bracket under pressure from a long context.
slides.title: 'Reply With JSON' Is a Suggestion, Not a Guarantee

bullets: Each state in the automaton tracks exactly which tokens are legal next, given what's been generated so far
At every decode step, logits for every token NOT legal from the current state get set to -infinity before sampling
The model is free to choose among whatever remains — it simply cannot emit anything that breaks the grammar
slides.body: Turn the target schema into a finite-state machine (or pushdown automaton for recursive structures) over the model's own vocabulary, ahead of generation.
slides.title: Compile the Schema Into a Token-Level Grammar

bullets: Vocabulary-to-transition mapping is precomputed once per schema
Each decode step then does a cheap state lookup to get the current valid-token mask
Implementations: Outlines and Guidance (regex/CFG-based), llama.cpp's GBNF grammars, vLLM and TensorRT-LLM's structured-output backends
No training or fine-tuning step required — this is a decoding-time constraint, not a model change
slides.body: The expensive part (compiling the schema into an automaton) happens once, before generation starts — not per token.
slides.title: Where the Masking Actually Happens

rows: Low — can still fail after retries
High, but only for trained schemas

slides.title: Three Ways to Get Structured Output

bullets: Grammar state says: next token must open a string with a key from {name, age, email}
The model 'wants' to write a stray sentence like 'Sure, here's the info:' first — every token that would start that sentence is masked to -infinity
After "age": the grammar only allows digit tokens or a closing structure — a model trying to write a word there finds every option masked out
End result: valid JSON every time, with zero retries and zero post-hoc parsing fixes
slides.body: Schema: {"name": string, "age": integer, "email": string}. The model is partway through generating, having just written the opening brace.
slides.title: Extracting a Name, Age, and Email From a Resume

bullets: Constrains shape, not truth — a syntactically perfect JSON object can still contain a confidently wrong age or a hallucinated email address
Deeply nested or highly recursive schemas can measurably slow decoding, since the automaton gets larger and lookups costlier
An overly rigid schema can hurt output quality by forcing the model into a structure that doesn't fit what it actually 'wants' to say
Skip it for open-ended creative writing or free-form chain-of-thought reasoning, where there's no fixed shape to enforce
Core idea worth remembering: when you can define the valid output space ahead of time, enforce it at the token level instead of hoping the model gets it right
slides.title: What It Fixes, and What It Can't

questions.explanation: Constrained decoding precompiles the schema into a token-level automaton and, at every decode step, sets the logits of any token that would break the schema to -infinity — so the model can only sample from tokens that keep the output valid.
questions.prompt: What does structured (constrained) decoding actually do at each generation step?
options: Masks the logits of every token that would violate the schema, leaving only valid tokens samplable
Fine-tunes the model on examples of valid JSON before generating
Generates the full response, then retries if it fails to parse
Translates the model's output into JSON after generation completes

questions.explanation: The grammar only constrains the shape of the output (correct keys, correct types, well-formed brackets). It has no way to check whether the actual values the model fills in are true or correct.
questions.prompt: Why is 'guarantees syntax, not semantics' an important limitation of structured decoding?
options: Because the output can be perfectly valid JSON while still containing factually wrong or hallucinated values
Because structured decoding only works with XML, not JSON
Because it requires the model to be fine-tuned first
Because it only works on closed-source models

questions.explanation: Structured decoding only helps when you can define the valid output space ahead of time as a schema or grammar. Open-ended tasks like creative writing or exploratory reasoning don't have a fixed shape to constrain against.
questions.prompt: When is structured decoding the wrong tool to reach for?
options: For open-ended creative writing or free-form reasoning, where there's no fixed output shape to enforce
For extracting a fixed set of fields from unstructured text
For tool-calling in an agent pipeline
For any task involving JSON output

posts.title: Mixture of Experts: Routing Tokens Instead of Scaling Dense
posts.subtitle: Most of a trillion-parameter model stays asleep on every token — only a handful of experts wake up.
posts.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures replace a transformer's dense feed-forward block with many smaller 'expert' sub-networks plus a learned router that activates only a handful of them per token. That lets models like Mixtral 8x7B and DeepSeek-V3 carry far more total knowledge than a dense model at similar compute cost per token — at the price of still needing every expert loaded in memory, plus real training and serving engineering to keep routing balanced.

bullets: Mixtral 8x7B: 46.7B total parameters, only ~12.9B active per token
DeepSeek-V3: 671B total parameters, only ~37B active per token
The trick: a learned router sends each token to a handful of specialist sub-networks
slides.title: Route the Token, Don't Scale the Whole Network

slides.body: A dense 70B model spends all 70B parameters on every single token it processes, whether or not that token needs anywhere near that much computation. Capacity and per-token compute are welded together — you can't add knowledge without also adding latency and cost.
slides.title: Dense Models Pay Full Price on Every Token

bullets: Top-2 routing (Mixtral) or top-1 (the original Switch Transformer): only 1-2 of N experts fire per token
A capacity factor caps how many tokens any single expert can take per batch; overflow tokens get dropped or passed through unchanged
An auxiliary load-balancing loss penalizes a router that keeps favoring the same few experts, to stop the rest of the network going unused ('expert collapse')
slides.body: Each transformer layer's dense feed-forward network is replaced by N smaller expert networks and a tiny router (a linear layer + softmax) that scores all N experts per token and activates only the top few.
slides.title: Swap the Feed-Forward Block for a Router + Experts

bullets: Total parameters: 46.7B, all of which must sit in accelerator memory
Router picks the top-2 experts for every token
Active compute per token: ~12.9B parameters worth of FLOPs — close to a dense 13B model's inference cost
Result: roughly a dense-13B compute bill for closer to a dense-47B model's knowledge capacity
slides.body: 8 experts, each roughly 7B parameters, inside the feed-forward layers, alongside shared attention and embedding layers.
slides.title: Mixtral 8x7B, Worked Through
Same Compute Budget, Very Different Capacity

bullets: Every expert must stay resident in memory, since any token could route to any of them — MoE's memory footprint tracks TOTAL parameters, not active ones
Without a load-balancing loss, training can collapse onto a handful of favorite experts, wasting the rest of the network's capacity
Serving at scale needs expert parallelism — routing is data-dependent, so communication between devices is uneven and harder to schedule than dense tensor parallelism
Not worth the complexity for small models or single-request low-latency serving, where memory bandwidth — not compute — is already the bottleneck
slides.title: The Catch: Memory Doesn't Shrink, Only Compute Does

questions.explanation: Top-2 routing fires exactly 2 of the 8 experts per token. The other 6 stay idle for that token — that gap between 'available' and 'active' is where the compute savings come from.
questions.prompt: In a top-2 Mixture-of-Experts layer with 8 experts, how many experts actually run for any given token?

questions.explanation: MoE cuts per-token compute, not memory. Since any token might route to any expert, all experts have to be resident in memory — Mixtral's 46.7B total parameters all need to be loaded even though only ~12.9B are active per token.
questions.prompt: Why doesn't a Mixture-of-Experts model use less GPU memory than a dense model with the same active-parameter count?
options: Because every expert must stay loaded in memory even though only a few run per token
Because MoE models require larger batch sizes to be efficient
Because the router network is larger than all the experts combined
Because MoE models are incompatible with quantization

questions.explanation: Without it, the router tends to settle early on a few experts it finds easy to optimize, which then get all the training signal while the remaining experts stay undertrained. The load-balancing term spreads tokens more evenly across experts during training.
questions.prompt: What does an auxiliary load-balancing loss prevent during MoE training?
options: The router collapsing onto a small subset of favorite experts, starving the rest of useful gradient signal
Overfitting on the training dataset
Gradient explosion in the attention layers
The model from routing to too few experts per token by design

posts.title: Your Transformer Is Secretly Thinking Two Thoughts
posts.subtitle: Average two unrelated text embeddings and a frozen LLM predicts both next tokens at once — an architectural property, not a trained skill.
posts.summary: A new interpretability paper shows that averaging the token embeddings of two unrelated text streams and feeding the mixture into an unmodified LLM produces a decodable superposition of both streams' next-token predictions. The authors call this the Superposition Linearity Hypothesis, show it's strongest early in pretraining and fades as training continues, and demonstrate a lightweight fine-tune plus guided decoding procedure that can partially recover two coherent continuations from a single forward pass — at a real cost to single-stream quality.

bullets: Average the token embeddings of two unrelated documents, position by position
Feed that averaged mixture into a standard, completely unmodified LLM
Both original next-token predictions still show up in the output — simultaneously
slides.title: One Forward Pass, Two Hidden Predictions

bullets: No gradient update, no special architecture, no retraining — just an averaged input
Tested across multiple model families: Pythia, Qwen2.5, and Llama checkpoints
slides.body: A transformer is a tower of nonlinear attention and MLP blocks. The default intuition: average two embeddings and you get noise somewhere between the two concepts — not two separate, recoverable predictions. The paper's central claim pushes directly against that intuition.
slides.title: Transformers Are Nonlinear. This Shouldn't Work.

bullets: Unmodified models: the true next token for BOTH streams lands in the merged top-10 about 30-40% of the time, versus a 2.63% random baseline
Top-100 recovery reaches 60-65%, versus a 10.41% baseline
The effect is strongest early in pretraining and decays as training progresses — evidence it's an intrinsic architectural property, not something the model learns to do
slides.body: When two token streams are linearly combined (element-wise embedding averaging), the model's output is approximately a superposition of the two individual next-token distributions — as if it ran both streams and blended the answers.
slides.title: The Superposition Linearity Hypothesis

bullets: Average the embeddings of 'The capital of France is' and 'The chemical symbol for gold is', token by token
A dense model would collapse this into one blurry prediction
A superposed model keeps both 'Paris' and 'Au' with meaningful probability mass in the same output distribution
slides.body: The paper tests this with real document pairs, not prompts like this — but the mechanism it describes plays out the same way on any two unrelated continuations.
slides.title: What the Mechanism Predicts, Illustrated

slides.body: A lightweight fine-tune (using under 0.025% of the original pretraining data) with KL self-distillation sharpens the superposition into something closer to two clean streams — but single-stream quality pays for it.

rows: Qwen2.5-3B: median rank of correct token

slides.title: Fine-Tuning Recovers It — At a Price

bullets: Theoretical framing: roughly 2x inference throughput and half the KV-cache footprint per active stream, since one pass serves two streams
In practice, a fused two-head decoder on Llama-3B hit 81.5 tokens/sec
A plain batch-size-2 baseline already hits 81.4 tokens/sec — the fused approach barely beats simple batching
Sequential (one-stream-at-a-time) decoding was the slow outlier at 41.3 tokens/sec
slides.body: The authors add a guided decoding procedure that disentangles the superposed output back into two separate, coherent continuations from a single forward pass.
slides.title: A Decoder That Un-Mixes the Two Streams

bullets: The throughput win over naive batching is marginal (81.5 vs 81.4 tok/s) — today this is an interpretability finding, not a deployment trick
Recovering clean dual-stream decoding costs real single-stream quality: FineWeb perplexity on Qwen2.5 jumped from 12.44 to 65.52 after the fine-tune
Evaluated only on contexts up to 128 tokens, and not tested on multimodal models — don't assume it generalizes to long-context or vision-language settings
Don't reach for this to 'double your throughput' in production; reach for it to understand why models sometimes blend unrelated context
slides.title: Pitfalls: Why This Isn't a Free Lunch Yet

questions.explanation: That's the paper's core finding: the merged output isn't gibberish — both streams' true next tokens remain detectable with far higher probability than chance, as if the model ran both in parallel and blended the results.
questions.prompt: What does the Superposition Linearity Hypothesis claim happens when you average the token embeddings of two unrelated text streams?
options: The model's output approximates a superposition of both streams' individual next-token distributions
The model throws an error because embeddings must come from a single stream
The model always predicts the first stream's token and ignores the second
The output collapses into random noise with no recoverable signal from either stream

questions.explanation: The authors observe the effect is strongest early in training and fades as pretraining continues, which they take as evidence that superposition is an intrinsic architectural property rather than a skill the model acquires through learning.
questions.prompt: What happens to this superposition property over the course of normal pretraining?
options: It decays as pretraining progresses
It only appears after pretraining is fully complete
It strengthens monotonically with more pretraining
It is unaffected by the amount of pretraining

questions.explanation: Despite a theoretical ~2x throughput framing, the measured fused two-head decoder (81.5 tok/s) essentially tied the plain batch-size-2 baseline (81.4 tok/s) on Llama-3B — the real-world win over ordinary batching is marginal today.
questions.prompt: How much faster was the paper's fused two-head decoder than simply running two requests at batch size 2?
options: Barely faster at all — 81.5 vs 81.4 tokens/sec
About 10x faster
Exactly 2x faster, matching the theoretical throughput claim
Slower than batch-size-2, making it impractical

references.title: Your Transformer Can Hold Two Thoughts at Once: Evidence of Linear Superposition in LLMs (arXiv:2609.29845)

posts.title: Claude Sonnet 5.5: Same Price Tag, Fewer Billable Tokens
posts.subtitle: Anthropic's mid-tier model gets 30% faster without raising the price per token
posts.summary: Claude Sonnet 5.5 keeps Sonnet 5's exact per-token pricing but runs 30%+ faster and needs fewer tokens and tool calls per task, so real-world cost drops anyway. It also launches with Opus-5.5-grade cyber safeguards and Sonnet's first distillation-defense classifiers.

slides.title: A mid-tier model that got faster, not pricier
slides.body: Anthropic announced Claude Sonnet 5.5 on September 28, 2026, built on the same foundation as Opus 5.5.
bullets: Available now on the Anthropic API, AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure
Developers call it via the model id claude-sonnet-5-5
Also ships with zero data retention as an enterprise option

slides.title: Frontier upgrades usually mean a bigger bill
slides.body: A faster, more capable model release typically comes with a higher per-token rate — the extra capability has to be paid for somewhere.
bullets: Sonnet 5.5 keeps Sonnet 5's exact rate card: $2 per million input tokens, $10 per million output tokens
Cache reads stay at $0.20/M, cache writes at $2.50/M — unchanged
So where does the claimed 'up to 30% less for most work' actually come from?

slides.title: The trick: spend fewer tokens, not cheaper ones
slides.body: Anthropic's framing is explicit — the savings come from the model needing fewer tokens and fewer tool calls to finish the same task, not from a discount.
bullets: Output generation is 30%+ faster than Sonnet 5
Fewer back-and-forth tool calls per task means less billed context to re-process
Net effect: same $/token rate, lower $/task in practice

slides.title: Sonnet 5 vs. Sonnet 5.5, by the numbers
Safety moved up a tier too
slides.body: Sonnet 5.5 inherits safeguards that used to be Opus-only, because its raw capability jumped enough to need them.
bullets: Cyber capabilities are now comparable to Opus 5.5's — with matching safeguards
Higher-risk cyber tasks automatically fall back to the older Sonnet 5 instead of being served by 5.5
First Sonnet model to ship safety classifiers specifically meant to block reasoning-extraction (distillation) attempts
Biology safeguards stay at the same level as Sonnet 5

slides.title: Worked example: a multi-file bug fix
slides.body: Picture an agent fixing a bug that spans three files and needs to run the test suite twice before it's confident.
bullets: On Sonnet 5: locate bug, edit, run tests, re-read failure, edit again, run tests — many tool calls, each one billed context
On Sonnet 5.5: the model needs fewer exploratory tool calls to converge on the same fix, at the same $2/$10 per-million rate
Fewer round-trips at an unchanged price is exactly where the 'up to 30% less' comes from in a coding-agent workload

slides.title: What to watch before you switch
slides.body: Sonnet 5.5 isn't a strict, unconditional upgrade for every workload.
bullets: The big FrontierCode number (46.2%) is reported at 'Max effort' — expect more latency/compute at that setting, not the default
A version-over-version benchmark jump this large (10.3% → 70.6% on Terminal-Bench) is worth checking against — is the benchmark itself versioned too (4.0 here), not just the model?
For the hardest reasoning tasks, Opus 5.5 is still the tier above Sonnet — Sonnet 5.5 targets well-scoped everyday work, bug fixes, and polished documents
Core idea to keep: cost per task, not cost per token, is the number that actually matters for agentic workloads

questions.prompt: Why does Anthropic say Sonnet 5.5 costs 'up to 30% less for most work' when its per-token price is identical to Sonnet 5?
options: Anthropic quietly lowered the per-token rate for most customers
It needs fewer tokens and tool calls to finish the same task, so the total task cost drops even though the rate per token doesn't
It only applies to batch API requests processed overnight
Output tokens are billed at half price during a launch promotion
questions.explanation: The $2/$10 per-million rate is unchanged from Sonnet 5. The savings are a side effect of efficiency — less generated/reprocessed context per task — not a price cut.

questions.prompt: What's new about Sonnet 5.5's safety posture compared to earlier Sonnet models?
options: It's the first Sonnet model to ship safety classifiers meant to block reasoning-extraction (distillation) attempts
It removes all cybersecurity-related safeguards to simplify the model
It applies Opus-level biology safeguards for the first time
It disables tool use entirely for high-risk prompts
questions.explanation: Because its cyber capability now rivals Opus 5.5's, Sonnet 5.5 needed Opus-grade safeguards — including a first-for-Sonnet defense against extracting its reasoning via distillation. Biology safeguards, by contrast, stayed at the Sonnet 5 level.

questions.prompt: Sonnet 5.5 scores 70.6% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 versus Sonnet 5's 10.3%. What should a careful reader check before concluding the model got 7x better at terminal tasks?
options: Whether the test was run on a faster CPU
Whether Terminal-Bench 4.0 is a revised/harder version of the benchmark, so the two scores aren't measuring an identical task set
Whether the score includes partial credit
Nothing — benchmark jumps this large are always directly comparable
questions.explanation: A benchmark's own version number (4.0 here) can change what's being measured. Huge jumps are a cue to check whether the eval itself shifted before reading the gap as pure model improvement.

posts.title: ZGCM-1: A 7B Model Built to Think, Not Memorize
posts.subtitle: A fully open 7.39B model pairs hybrid attention and FP8 training to punch above its parameter count on math and agentic search
posts.summary: ZGCM-1 is a fully open 7.39B-parameter dense model trained from scratch for math and agentic search. It combines gated sliding-window/global hybrid attention with an FP8 Muon optimizer to hit roughly 4.2x better pretraining efficiency and 3.94x training throughput at 256K context, releasing every checkpoint, dataset, and training script under MIT.

slides.title: Small model, deliberately not a small encyclopedia
slides.body: ZGCM-1 is a 7.39B dense language model trained from scratch, built for mathematical reasoning and agentic search rather than broad recall.
bullets: Fully open: per-stage weights, intermediate checkpoints, training code, data recipes, and eval harness are all public
MIT-licensed; model on Hugging Face as zgcagi/ZGCM-1-7B
32-layer decoder-only Transformer, 4,096 hidden size, 32 query heads / 8 KV heads

slides.title: A 7B model can't out-memorize the open web
slides.body: The paper's core premise: compact models hit a hard parametric capacity ceiling if their only strategy is storing facts.
bullets: Math and agentic search both need precise multi-step reasoning, not recall of a fact that happened to appear in training data
Scaling parameters to fix this is the obvious answer but defeats the point of a small, open, cheap-to-run model
ZGCM-1's bet: couple deliberate internal 'thinking' with active external tool use instead of brute-force memorization

slides.title: Hybrid attention: mostly local, occasionally global
slides.body: Of the 32 attention layers, 27 use gated sliding-window attention and only 5 use full global attention.
bullets: Sliding-window layers are cheap at long context; the 5 global layers preserve long-range information flow across the sequence
Context length: 262,144 tokens (256K) reached via progressive mid-training: 16K → 64K → 256K
Training uses FP8 precision paired with the Muon optimizer, chosen for stability at low precision
SFT stage jointly mixes general instruction data with agentic tool-use examples, in both 'thinking' and direct-response modes

slides.title: What the hybrid design actually buys
Worked example: a problem the model can't just recall
slides.body: Task: compute a multi-step word problem that hinges on a specific numeric fact (say, a conversion rate) the model doesn't reliably remember.
bullets: A pure-recall approach guesses the constant from training data and risks a wrong answer with high confidence
ZGCM-1's SFT mixes in agentic tool-use examples, so the trained behavior is to pause mid-reasoning and issue a tool call (e.g., a calculator or lookup) for the uncertain fact
The 5 global-attention layers keep that tool result visible to the rest of the reasoning chain, even if the call happened many tokens earlier in a long context

slides.title: Where this design is the wrong fit
slides.body: The efficiency gains are real but relative — they don't make this a free lunch.
bullets: Still trained from scratch on ~4.19T + 600B tokens — a serious compute budget, just a more efficient one
27 sliding-window layers trade some long-range attention fidelity for speed; only 5 global layers compensate, so very long-range dependencies outside those layers' reach can still get lossy
Specialized for math and agentic search — not positioned as a general-purpose chat model
Core idea to keep: when you can't afford more parameters, spend the capacity you have on deciding when to think longer or call a tool, instead of trying to memorize more

questions.prompt: What lets ZGCM-1 report 3.94x training throughput at 256K context versus full attention?
options: Reducing the model to 8 total layers
A hybrid design: 27 gated sliding-window attention layers plus only 5 full global-attention layers out of 32
Dropping the KV cache entirely at long context
Training exclusively on short 4K-token sequences
questions.explanation: Sliding-window attention is far cheaper than full attention at long context; keeping just 5 global layers preserves long-range information flow without paying the full quadratic cost everywhere.

questions.prompt: Why pair FP8 precision specifically with the Muon optimizer rather than a standard optimizer like AdamW?
options: FP8 and Muon are unrelated; the pairing is arbitrary
Muon's update structure was chosen because low-precision (FP8) training is more prone to numerical instability, and Muon helps keep training stable at that precision
Muon only works with 256K context windows
AdamW cannot run on GPUs that support FP8
questions.explanation: FP8 training saves memory and compute but narrows numerical headroom. The paper credits the FP8+Muon combination, alongside the attention and normalization choices, for the reported ~4.2x pretraining efficiency gain without divergence.

questions.prompt: What is ZGCM-1's core design premise, per its own stated rationale?
options: A bigger context window can fully substitute for more parameters
Compact models can't passively memorize the open web, so they should couple deliberate internal thinking with active external tool use instead
Open-sourcing weights automatically improves benchmark scores
FP8 training alone is sufficient to match larger models' accuracy
questions.explanation: That's the premise stated directly in the project's own description: a 7B model can't out-memorize the web, so it should reason more deliberately and reach for tools instead of guessing from recall.

posts.title: RoPE: Teaching Attention Where Things Are by Rotating Them
posts.subtitle: Rotary position embeddings bake relative position straight into the attention dot product — at zero extra parameters
posts.summary: Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) rotate each query/key vector by an angle proportional to its position, so the attention dot product naturally depends only on relative distance between tokens. Used across LLaMA, Qwen, Mistral and GPT-NeoX-family models, it generalizes better than learned absolute embeddings but still needs tricks like position interpolation or YaRN to extend far beyond its trained context length.

slides.title: Position, encoded as a rotation
slides.body: RoPE is the positional encoding scheme behind most modern open-weight LLMs — LLaMA, Qwen, Mistral, and the GPT-NeoX family all use it.
bullets: No learned position-embedding table — position is applied as a geometric transformation
Introduced in the 2021 RoFormer paper
The same mechanism that makes long-context extension tricks like YaRN possible

slides.title: Absolute position embeddings don't generalize
slides.body: The original Transformer added a fixed or learned position vector to each token embedding before attention.
bullets: Works fine up to the sequence length seen in training
Gives attention no direct signal about the *relative* distance between two tokens — it has to infer that indirectly
Extending to longer sequences at inference means extrapolating into position vectors the model never trained on

slides.title: The trick: rotate query and key by position
slides.body: Split each query/key vector into 2D pairs. Rotate pair i by an angle theta_i times the token's position, where theta_i shrinks geometrically across the pairs (like sinusoidal frequencies).
bullets: Both the query at position m and the key at position n get rotated before their dot product is taken
Rotation composition means that dot product collapses to depend only on the angle difference — i.e., on (m − n), not on m or n individually
Result: relative position falls out of the attention score for free, with zero added parameters

slides.title: RoPE vs. the alternatives

rows: Yes — built into the Q·K dot product
Yes — added as a distance-based bias

slides.title: Worked example: extending a 4K model to 32K
slides.body: Take a model trained with RoPE on a 4K-token context. Feed it an 8K-token document and quality degrades — the rotation angles at positions 4,001–8,000 exceed anything seen in training.
bullets: Position Interpolation: rescale positions by L_train / L_target (here 4096/32768) so the largest angle at inference matches the largest angle seen in training
NTK-aware / YaRN scaling: rescale the per-dimension frequencies instead of positions directly, preserving high-frequency (local) precision while stretching low-frequency (long-range) reach
Both let the same trained weights handle 32K input without retraining from scratch — at some cost to short-range precision

slides.title: When plain RoPE isn't enough
slides.body: RoPE fixes position encoding — it doesn't fix everything about long sequences.
bullets: Naive extrapolation past the trained context length degrades quality; it needs an explicit scaling method, not just a longer input
Interpolation and YaRN trade a bit of short-context sharpness for long-context reach — not a pure win
RoPE doesn't address attention's quadratic compute cost — that's why it's often paired with sliding-window or hybrid attention (as in efficient long-context models) rather than used alone
Core idea to keep: relative position can be a geometric property of the vectors themselves, not a separate thing you add to them

questions.prompt: What property does RoPE give the attention mechanism 'for free' through its rotation trick?
options: The attention score between two positions depends only on their relative distance, not their absolute positions
Attention becomes linear instead of quadratic in sequence length
Every token attends equally to every other token regardless of position
The model no longer needs a key or value projection
questions.explanation: Rotating both query and key by their respective positions makes the composed rotation in their dot product depend only on the angle difference — i.e., the relative offset (m − n) — not on either absolute position.

questions.prompt: Why does a model trained with RoPE on a 4K context often degrade badly on much longer inputs without any adjustment?
options: RoPE requires a learned embedding table that runs out of entries
The rotation angles at those longer positions fall outside the range the model ever saw during training
Longer inputs automatically increase the model's parameter count
RoPE only works for inputs shorter than 1,000 tokens
questions.explanation: RoPE has no hard length limit baked in, but the model's weights were only tuned for the range of rotation angles seen during training — angles far outside that range behave unpredictably.

questions.prompt: What do Position Interpolation and YaRN actually change to extend a RoPE model's usable context?
options: They add new transformer layers for the extra length
They rescale the positions or per-dimension frequencies so long-sequence rotation angles map back into the range the model was trained on
They replace RoPE entirely with a learned embedding table
They truncate the input to fit the original context length
questions.explanation: Both are scaling tricks applied to the same RoPE formula — one rescales positions directly, the other rescales frequencies — so the model keeps operating within familiar angle ranges instead of extrapolating blindly.

references.title: RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding (arXiv:2104.09864)

posts.title: τ0-VLA: A Robot That Plans Before It Moves
posts.subtitle: A hierarchical foundation model that searches a learned world model before committing to the next move
posts.summary: τ0-VLA splits robot control into a high-level planner that searches a learned world model for the best next subtask, and a low-level flow-matching policy that executes it. Trained on 40,115 hours of real robot data, it's open-weighted under Apache 2.0.

slides.title: Robots that deliberate, not just react
slides.body: τ0-VLA is a hierarchical robot foundation model from sii-research: a planner that thinks, and an executor that acts, trained on over 40,000 hours of real-world robot data.
bullets: Open weights, Apache 2.0 license
Code, weights, and training data format all public
Built on a Qwen3.5 vision-language backbone

slides.title: Flat policies drift over long horizons
slides.body: Most vision-language-action (VLA) models are 'flat': one network maps pixels straight to motor commands, step by step, with no deliberation in between.
bullets: Great at single skills (grasp, pour, place) in isolation
Errors compound silently across a long multi-step task
No mechanism to stop, reconsider, or search for a better next move

slides.title: Two policies, two jobs
slides.body: τ0-VLA splits control into a memory-augmented high-level policy that proposes the next subtask, and a generalist low-level policy that executes it.
bullets: Low-level policy: Qwen3.5 VLM backbone + Mixture-of-Transformers action expert
Actions generated via conditional flow matching over a unified 40-dimensional state/action space
Trained on 40,115 hours of heterogeneous real-world robot data (LeRobot v3.0 format, incl. AgiBot World)

slides.title: The twist: searching before acting
slides.body: The high-level policy doesn't just emit one guess for the next subtask — it uses a learned world model to simulate candidate subtasks and picks the one that scores best, spending extra compute at inference time instead of just training time.
bullets: This is 'test-time computation': quality bought at answer-time, not just train-time
More deliberation when the situation is ambiguous; less when it's obvious
Mirrors how LLM reasoning models search over candidate solutions before answering

slides.title: Flat VLA vs. hierarchical + search

rows: Implicit, baked into one forward pass
Explicit subtask proposed by a separate policy

slides.title: Worked example: making a drink, start to finish
slides.body: Task: 'make a cup of coffee.' The high-level policy doesn't hard-code the subtask sequence — it searches at each decision point.
bullets: Step 1: simulate candidates ('grab mug' vs 'turn on machine first') against the world model, pick the better-scoring order
Step 2: hand 'grab mug' to the low-level policy, which executes via flow matching over the 40-dim action space
Step 3: after each subtask, re-plan — if the mug was already out, skip straight to the machine
This re-planning loop is what lets the system recover from an unexpected state instead of blindly continuing a fixed script

slides.title: When this is the wrong tool
slides.body: Hierarchical search isn't free — it costs latency and compute, and it needs a world model good enough to trust.
bullets: Simple single-step pick-and-place: the search overhead buys nothing — use a flat policy
If the world model is inaccurate, the planner can confidently pick a bad subtask — garbage-in, garbage-out
40k+ hours of multi-embodiment data is expensive to collect — not a recipe you bootstrap cheaply
Core idea to keep: separate 'what to do next' from 'how to do it', and spend more thought when the task actually needs it

questions.prompt: What problem does τ0-VLA's hierarchical split (high-level + low-level policy) mainly address?
options: Reducing the size of the vision-language backbone
Error compounding over long multi-step tasks that a single flat policy can't recover from
Making the model cheaper to train on a single GPU
Removing the need for any real robot data
questions.explanation: A flat policy has no way to notice or correct drift across a long task. Separating 'decide the next subtask' from 'execute it' gives the system a natural point to re-plan and recover.

questions.prompt: What does 'world-model-guided test-time computation' mean in this context?
options: The model is retrained on new data at test time
The high-level policy simulates candidate subtasks against a learned world model and picks the best-scoring one before acting
The robot pauses to download updated weights before each task
The low-level policy skips flow matching during evaluation
questions.explanation: Instead of training the only way to get a better answer, extra computation is spent at inference time — searching over options with a world model — the same philosophy behind reasoning-heavy LLM techniques.

questions.prompt: When would τ0-VLA's approach be overkill?
options: A long-horizon task with many possible failure points
A single-step pick-and-place task with no ambiguity about what to do next
A task that spans multiple robot embodiments
A task requiring recovery from an unexpected state
questions.explanation: The search-and-replan machinery earns its cost on long, ambiguous, multi-step tasks. For a single obvious action, a flat policy does the same job for a fraction of the latency and compute.

posts.title: Bilibili Open-Sources Index-Translate for 150 Languages
posts.subtitle: A full open-weight translation family — text, speech, dubbing, and long documents — under Apache 2.0

slides.title: Frontier translation, fully open
slides.body: On September 30, Bilibili's Index LLM team released Index-Translate: a family of multilingual translation models built on Qwen3.5, covering 150 languages, released under Apache 2.0.
bullets: 2B, 9B, and 35B-A3B (MoE, preview) sizes
Weights on Hugging Face and ModelScope
Technical report, code, and an online demo all public

slides.title: Good translation has stayed mostly closed
slides.body: The strongest multilingual translation quality has largely lived behind closed commercial APIs, while open general-purpose LLMs aren't specifically tuned for translation fidelity, timing, or document-scale consistency.
bullets: Closed APIs: hard to self-host, audit, or fine-tune further
General LLMs: not optimized for terminology consistency across a long document
Dubbing and speech translation need timing control that plain text models don't offer

slides.title: One family, four specialized siblings
slides.body: Built on Alibaba's Qwen3.5, the release isn't one model but a family targeting different translation jobs.
bullets: Index-Translate: core text translation, 150 languages, 2B/9B/35B-A3B
Index-Echo: speech-to-speech translation
Index-Homura: syllable-controlled translation for dub timing
Index-NativeLong: long-document translation, tested to 64K tokens

slides.title: Reported benchmark scores (9B tier)
Worked example: dubbing a video clip
slides.body: Say you're localizing a short video from Mandarin to Spanish for lip-synced dubbing.
bullets: Index-Translate converts the script, preserving meaning and tone
Index-Homura re-times the Spanish phrasing to land within 10% of the original syllable count, so mouth movement stays roughly in sync
Index-Echo can instead translate the speech audio directly, skipping the text step entirely
For a 64K-token script with recurring character names, Index-NativeLong keeps terminology consistent across the whole document

slides.title: Built for real deployment, not just a demo
slides.body: The release shipped with production concerns already handled.
bullets: GGUF builds for local inference via llama.cpp
FP8 (W8A8) and NVFP4 (W4A4, Blackwell-optimized) builds for vLLM serving
October 4: free, OpenAI-compatible public API endpoints for the 35B-A3B model

slides.title: What to watch before you deploy it
slides.body: Open and capable doesn't mean free of tradeoffs.
bullets: 35B-A3B is explicitly a 'preview' — only 3B of the 35B parameters activate per token, but you still need enough VRAM to hold all the experts
Homura trades literal accuracy for timing fit — wrong tool when exact meaning matters more than lip-sync (legal, medical)
Benchmark scores above are the project's own reported numbers, not an independent third-party eval
Biggest win: a fully open, deployable translation stack with per-use-case specialized siblings instead of one generic model

questions.prompt: Index-Translate-35B-A3B is a Mixture-of-Experts model. What does the 'A3B' tell you?
options: The model was trained on 3 billion tokens total
Only 3B of the 35B total parameters are active per token, even though all experts must still fit in memory
The model runs 3x faster than the 9B dense version
It supports 3 billion languages
questions.explanation: MoE models activate a small subset of experts per token (3B here) while the full parameter count (35B) still needs to be loaded — compute scales with active params, memory scales with total params.

questions.prompt: Which sibling model would you reach for to keep character names consistent across a 64K-token document?
options: Index-Echo
Index-Homura
Index-NativeLong
Index-Translate-2B
questions.explanation: Index-NativeLong is the sibling specifically evaluated on long-document translation (GuoFeng @ 64K tokens), where maintaining terminology consistency across the whole document is the core challenge.

questions.prompt: When is Index-Homura's syllable-controlled translation the wrong choice?
options: When dubbing a video and lip-sync timing matters
When translating a legal contract where exact meaning must be preserved over timing
When the target language has a different syllable structure than the source
When translating short phrases
questions.explanation: Homura optimizes phrasing to hit a target syllable count for dub timing, which can nudge wording away from the most literally precise translation — a bad fit when fidelity matters more than timing.

posts.title: Test-Time Compute: Buying Accuracy at Inference
posts.subtitle: Why sampling, search, and longer reasoning at answer-time can beat a bigger model
posts.summary: Test-time compute scaling spends extra computation at inference — sampling, search, or extended reasoning — instead of growing the model, often recovering accuracy a single greedy pass misses. The gains are real but come with latency and cost tradeoffs, and they saturate on easy problems.

slides.title: More thinking, same model
slides.body: For years, a better answer meant a bigger model trained on more data. Test-time compute takes a different lever: keep the model fixed, spend more computation at the moment it answers.
bullets: Not a training technique — a decoding-time technique
Trades latency and $ per query for accuracy
Behind reasoning-heavy models like o1 and R1-style systems

slides.title: A single greedy pass often knows better than it shows
slides.body: A model frequently has the right answer somewhere in its output distribution — it just doesn't surface on the first, cheapest attempt.
bullets: Hard reasoning problems have many ways to slip (one arithmetic error, one skipped case)
Greedy decoding commits to the first plausible path and never looks back
The fix doesn't require more parameters — it requires more attempts or more deliberation

slides.title: Four ways to spend the extra compute
bullets: Best-of-N: sample N full answers, use a verifier/reward model to pick the best
Self-consistency: sample N reasoning chains, take the majority-vote final answer
Search (beam / MCTS): explore and prune reasoning steps guided by a process reward model
Extended chain-of-thought: generate a long internal 'thinking' trace before committing to a final answer (o1/R1-style)

slides.title: How to spend the budget matters more than how much
slides.body: Research on compute-optimal test-time scaling (e.g. Snell et al.) found that for a fixed inference budget, the best allocation — more samples vs. deeper search vs. longer reasoning — depends on how hard the problem is.
bullets: Easy problems saturate fast: extra samples past a point add no accuracy
Hard problems benefit more from search/verification than from raw sampling
A well-tuned small model with the right test-time strategy can match a much larger model run once

slides.title: Picking a technique

rows: Tasks with a cheap, reliable verifier
Problems with a clear final answer to vote on
Multi-step reasoning with checkable intermediate steps
Open-ended reasoning without a separate verifier

slides.title: Worked example: a competition math problem
slides.body: A hard AIME-style problem: a single greedy solve makes one arithmetic slip midway and lands on the wrong final number.
bullets: Run the model 32 times independently (best-of-N / self-consistency)
28 of 32 attempts converge on the same final answer — the slip was attempt-specific, not systematic
Majority vote (or a verifier scoring each attempt) surfaces the correct answer that any single run had a real chance of missing
Same idea, different domain: τ0-VLA's robot planner searches candidate subtasks against a world model before committing — test-time compute applied to action planning instead of math

slides.title: Know the limits before reaching for it
slides.body: Test-time compute is a real lever, not a free one.
bullets: Cost multiplies with N — 32 samples is roughly 32x the tokens of one pass
Gains saturate: past a point, more samples or deeper search barely move accuracy
Self-consistency without a verifier just votes — if the model is systematically wrong, the majority is wrong too
Skip it for easy, low-stakes queries where one pass is already reliable — the extra cost buys nothing

questions.prompt: What is the core idea behind test-time compute scaling?
options: Train a larger model on more data
Spend more computation at inference time (sampling, search, longer reasoning) instead of growing the model
Quantize the model to run faster
Fine-tune the model on the specific test question
questions.explanation: Test-time compute keeps the trained model fixed and instead spends extra computation when answering — through sampling, search, or extended reasoning — to recover accuracy a single pass would miss.

questions.prompt: Which technique relies on a verifier or reward model to choose among several full candidate answers?
options: Self-consistency
Best-of-N
Greedy decoding
Extended chain-of-thought alone
questions.explanation: Best-of-N generates N complete answers and uses a separate verifier/reward model to score and pick the best one, unlike self-consistency which just votes on the final answer without a learned scorer.

questions.prompt: When should you avoid spending extra test-time compute on a query?
options: When the problem is a hard multi-step reasoning task
When the query is easy and low-stakes, and a single pass is already reliable
When you have a good process reward model available
When the model has a long context window
questions.explanation: Extra sampling or search multiplies latency and cost. On easy, low-stakes queries a single greedy pass is already accurate, so the extra spend buys little to nothing.

posts.title: NeoHorse-1: A Model That Routes Its Own Training Data
posts.subtitle: Recursive self-improvement, powered by a routing harness instead of a bigger model
posts.summary: NeoHorse-1 post-trains Qwen3.5-4B/9B using a routing harness that treats 'which model tier actually served a request' as a free capability signal, feeding it back into the training mix. Across ten benchmarks, macro averages rose from 58.94 to 64.87 (4B) and 65.60 to 69.04 (9B), making it the top trending paper on Hugging Face Daily Papers in early October 2026.

slides.title: A Model That Decides What It Needs to Learn Next
slides.body: NeoHorse-1 is the top trending paper on Hugging Face right now — and its core idea is almost mundane: route each real interaction to the right capability tier, then feed that back into training.

slides.title: Static Fine-Tuning Datasets Waste a Free Signal
slides.body: Most agentic post-training throws the same fixed dataset at every model size, even though which model actually gets used in production already reveals where its capability ends.
bullets: Standard pipeline: collect demonstrations once, fine-tune every checkpoint on the same mix
A served model's successes and failures show exactly what it can and can't handle — most pipelines never feed that back in
Result: a 4B model gets trained on data mismatched to what it's actually ready to learn next

slides.title: A Routing Harness Turns Usage Into Curriculum
slides.body: NeoHorse-1 organizes every interaction into three levels — trajectories, user turns, and subscenes (semantically grouped turns) — then a router estimates how much capability each turn actually demanded.
bullets: The router predicts capability demand per turn and which service tier should have handled it
That estimate reshapes the supervised fine-tuning and on-policy-distillation mix for the next training round
Updated model reveals new strengths/weaknesses, the router re-estimates demand, and the cycle repeats — the paper's definition of recursive self-improvement here

slides.title: The Gap Between 4B and 9B Narrows
slides.body: Across ten benchmarks spanning harness-based agents, tool use, coding, and instruction-following, routing-harness-derived post-training lifted both checkpoints.

slides.title: What the Router Actually Buys You: A Debugging Loop
slides.body: The paper's qualitative analysis: the 4B model learns iterative debugging — write code, run it, read the error, patch it — while the 9B model develops a test-driven refine loop, writing its own tests before finalizing a fix.
bullets: A 4B coding agent hits a runtime error; the router had tagged similar failures as needing retry-with-feedback examples, so the model was over-sampled on exactly that pattern
Outcome: the 4B model shows failure-recovery behavior usually associated with much larger models

slides.title: Where the Routing Signal Gets Noisy
slides.body: The authors flag a real limitation: which model actually served a request is an imperfect proxy for what capability that request needed.
bullets: User overrides, rate-limit availability, and deployment policy all influence which tier handles a turn — not just task difficulty
That noise feeds into the next round's capability-demand estimate, and can compound across self-improvement cycles if uncorrected
'Recursive self-improvement' here means re-deriving the training mix from usage data, not a model rewriting its own weights unsupervised

slides.title: Key Takeaways
bullets: NeoHorse-1 treats 'which model tier handled this turn' as a free training signal — no new human labeling required
Post-training lifted the 10-benchmark macro average from 58.94 to 64.87 (4B) and 65.60 to 69.04 (9B) over the Qwen3.5 base
It was the top trending paper on Hugging Face Daily Papers in early October 2026
Biggest caveat: the routing signal is only as clean as the deployment data it's harvested from

questions.prompt: What signal does NeoHorse-1's routing harness use to build its training curriculum?
options: Human-labeled difficulty scores for every example
Which model tier actually served each real interaction, used as a proxy for capability demand
Random sampling across all available data
A separate reward model trained from scratch
questions.explanation: The router estimates capability demand from which model size actually handled a given turn in production, then uses that to reshape the training mix — turning deployment telemetry into curriculum instead of new human labels.

questions.prompt: By how much did the 9B model's 10-benchmark macro average improve after NeoHorse-1's post-training?
options: It stayed flat
It dropped slightly to improve safety
questions.explanation: The 9B checkpoint moved from a 65.60 base average to 69.04 post-training; the 4B checkpoint's corresponding jump was 58.94 to 64.87.

questions.prompt: What's the key caveat the authors raise about their own method?
options: It only works on coding benchmarks
It requires a 100B+ parameter router model
Which model served a request is an imperfect proxy for what capability it actually needed, since overrides and availability also play a role
It cannot be run on open-weight models
questions.explanation: The paper notes deployment factors like user overrides, rate-limit availability, and routing policy — not just task difficulty — influence which model handles a turn, adding noise to the capability-demand signal the whole approach depends on.

It monitors channels, tracks threads, executes recurring tasks, and can resume a project days later without a new prompt
You @mention it like a colleague across Teams, Outlook, chats, channels, and documents, governed by its own permissions and audit trail

posts.title: Agent Memory: Why a Context Window Isn't Enough
posts.subtitle: Working, episodic, and semantic memory — and how agents actually implement them
posts.summary: A context window is temporary working memory — it vanishes the moment a session ends or fills up. Real agents need episodic, semantic, and procedural memory on top of it, implemented through summarization, vector retrieval, and external scratchpads, each with its own failure modes like memory poisoning and context rot.

slides.title: A Context Window Is Not Memory
slides.body: Drop an agent's context window and it forgets everything instantly, including things it learned five minutes ago. Real memory means some of that survives on purpose.

slides.title: The Context Window Is Finite, Shared, and Forgetful
slides.body: Every tool call, retrieved document, and past turn competes for the same fixed token budget, and once it's full, something gets dropped or summarized away.
bullets: A 1M-token context sounds huge until an agent has run for days across hundreds of tool calls and documents
Even within budget, models attend less reliably to information buried in the middle of a long context
A session restart (new conversation, new process, new day) wipes the window completely unless something was saved outside it

slides.title: Four Kinds of Memory, Borrowed From Cognitive Science
slides.body: Agent frameworks typically distinguish memory by how long it lasts and what it holds.

rows: Raw tokens in the context window
Structured facts in a DB or knowledge graph
How to do a task (skills, tool-use patterns)
Fine-tuned weights or reusable skill libraries

slides.title: Compression Is the Real Engineering Problem
slides.body: You can't just append everything forever, so most production agents run some form of compression before information leaves the working-memory window.
bullets: Summarization: periodically collapse old turns into a shorter running summary, trading detail for space
Retrieval: store raw events as embeddings in a vector store and pull back only the most relevant ones when needed — the same mechanism as RAG, applied to the agent's own history
Scratchpad files: write structured notes/state to an external file or DB the agent re-reads, instead of keeping everything in-context
Most real systems combine all three: a scratchpad for durable facts, retrieval for 'have I seen this before,' summarization for everything else

slides.title: A Support Agent Across a Three-Day Ticket
slides.body: A customer's billing issue takes three days and six separate chat sessions to resolve.
bullets: Session 1: the agent writes a scratchpad note — 'customer on annual plan, disputing a prorated charge, waiting on finance' — to a ticket-memory store, not just the chat window
Session 4 (new day, empty context window): the agent retrieves that note via the ticket ID before replying, so it doesn't ask the customer to re-explain
By session 6, a semantic-memory layer has learned 'this customer prefers email summaries over chat' from past interactions, and applies it unprompted

slides.title: Memory Has Failure Modes Too
slides.body: Giving an agent memory doesn't just add capability, it adds new ways to go wrong.
bullets: Memory poisoning: a wrong fact written to long-term memory early on gets silently treated as ground truth in every later session
Context rot: stale retrieved memories crowd out more relevant, newer information if retrieval isn't ranked by recency as well as similarity
Privacy/compliance: persistent memory of user data needs the same retention, deletion, and audit rules as any other stored personal data
When NOT to bother: short-lived, single-turn tasks (one-shot classification, a single lookup) don't need episodic or semantic memory — the context window alone is simpler and cheaper

slides.title: Key Takeaways
bullets: Working memory is the context window; episodic, semantic, and procedural memory are what survive past it
The engineering problem is compression: summarize, retrieve, or externalize to a scratchpad, since raw context alone doesn't scale
Real agents mix multiple memory types; a single vector store is rarely the whole answer
Memory adds failure modes (poisoning, staleness, privacy) — don't add it to agents that never need to remember past one turn

questions.prompt: What's the key difference between an agent's context window and its 'memory'?
options: There is no difference, they're the same thing
The context window is a fixed, shared token budget for the current session; memory is information deliberately persisted beyond it
Memory only exists in multimodal agents
The context window is always larger than any memory store
questions.explanation: The context window holds what's active right now and disappears when the session ends or the window fills up; memory is specifically what an agent deliberately saves outside that window so it survives.

questions.prompt: Which technique is most directly borrowed from RAG to implement episodic memory?
options: Fine-tuning a new model per user
Summarization of old turns
Storing past events as embeddings in a vector store and retrieving the most relevant ones on demand
Increasing the context window size
questions.explanation: Episodic memory commonly reuses RAG's core mechanism: embed and store past events, then retrieve the top matches, just applied to the agent's own history instead of an external document set.

questions.prompt: What is 'memory poisoning' as a failure mode?
options: An agent running out of context window space
A security exploit that deletes an agent's memory store
A wrong fact written to long-term memory being silently treated as true in all future sessions
A model forgetting its system prompt
questions.explanation: If an incorrect fact gets written into persistent memory, retrieval keeps surfacing it as if it were verified truth in every later session, compounding the error instead of it fading away like an ordinary mistaken guess would.

posts.title: Finetuning with Sampling: SFT Learns Better Than You Think
posts.subtitle: A resampling trick lets plain SFT rival RL post-training
posts.summary: Harvard researchers show that supervised fine-tuning (SFT) underperforms RL post-training mainly because expert demonstration data is 'off-policy' relative to the base model. Their projection sampling algorithm resamples expert trajectories toward the base model's own distribution before SFT, letting plain SFT rival or beat RL and on-policy distillation on generalization and forgetting across chemistry, math, and medical QA tasks.

slides.body: A new paper from Harvard argues the real problem with supervised fine-tuning was never the algorithm — it was the data.
slides.title: SFT Isn't as Weak as Everyone Thinks

bullets: RL and on-policy distillation (OPSD) let the model learn from its *own* generated rollouts
Plain SFT instead forces the model toward trajectories it would never have produced itself
Conventional wisdom: if you want strong generalization, skip SFT and go straight to RL post-training
slides.body: Standard SFT trains on fixed expert demonstrations — written by humans or a stronger model. That data reflects someone else's token distribution, not the base model's own. The mismatch is why SFT often generalizes worse and forgets more than RL-style post-training.
slides.title: Expert Data Is 'Off-Policy'

bullets: MCMC resamples each expert trajectory toward higher likelihood under the base model
Keeps the 'privileged information' in expert data (correct reasoning, correct final answer)
Output is a dataset that looks like something the base model could plausibly have written itself
Then: completely standard SFT on this adjusted dataset — no new training objective needed
slides.body: The authors introduce projection sampling, a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) procedure that iteratively transforms off-policy expert traces to be more on-policy with respect to a reference (base) model — before any fine-tuning happens.
slides.title: Projection Sampling: Nudge the Data, Not the Model

slides.body: Evaluated across novel skill acquisition (chemistry), reasoning (math), and open-ended expertise (medical QA).
slides.title: How It Stacks Up Against RL-Style Post-Training

bullets: Naive approach: SFT directly on the expert traces — model memorizes surface patterns, struggles on held-out problems, forgets unrelated skills
Projection sampling approach: MCMC-resample each trace so it better matches what the base model would itself generate while still reaching the correct answer
Result reported: SFT on the resampled data generalizes to held-out test problems and preserves prior capabilities better than plain SFT, rivaling RL/OPSD
slides.body: A lab wants a base LLM to pick up a chemistry reasoning skill it currently lacks, using a set of expert-written solved problems.
slides.title: Teaching a Model New Chemistry Reasoning

bullets: MCMC resampling adds real compute overhead on top of plain SFT — you pay for it before training even starts
It needs access to the base/reference model's likelihoods during data prep, which plain SFT doesn't
It doesn't give you live reward signals or multi-turn environment interaction — settings that genuinely need RL still need RL
Benefits were shown on skill-acquisition and reasoning tasks; it's not evidence SFT always matches RL everywhere
slides.body: Projection sampling is a data-preparation step before SFT, not a universal replacement for RL.
slides.title: Where This Doesn't Help

bullets: A lot of SFT's reputed weakness traces back to data distribution mismatch, not the SFT objective itself
Projection sampling (MCMC) reshapes expert data to be more on-policy before standard SFT
Across chemistry, math, and medical QA, SFT+projection sampling rivaled RL and on-policy distillation on generalization and forgetting
Accepted to NeurIPS 2026 — a sign the result has held up to scrutiny
slides.title: Key Takeaways

questions.explanation: The paper's core claim is that the data, not the algorithm, is the bottleneck: expert traces come from a different distribution than what the base model would generate, and that mismatch hurts generalization.
questions.prompt: According to the paper, why does standard SFT often generalize worse than RL-style post-training?
options: SFT uses a fundamentally weaker loss function than RL

posts.title: Context Engineering: Deciding What the Model Actually Sees
posts.subtitle: Why curating an agent's context window matters more than wording its prompt
posts.summary: Context engineering is the discipline of actively managing everything that fills an LLM's context window across a multi-step task — what to retrieve, what to compress, what to isolate into sub-agents, and what to drop. As agents run longer and touch more tools, this matters more than how any single prompt is worded.

slides.body: A long-running agent doesn't fail because of one bad prompt — it fails because its context quietly fills with the wrong things.
slides.title: The Window Is Finite. Plan Like It.

bullets: Context windows are large but not infinite — and cost scales with every token you keep around
Models attend less reliably to information buried in the middle of a long context than to the start or end ('lost in the middle')
Irrelevant history doesn't just cost tokens — it actively distracts the model from the current step
slides.body: A coding agent making 50 tool calls can easily generate hundreds of thousands of tokens of file reads, command output, and intermediate reasoning.
slides.title: Agents Accumulate Context Fast

bullets: Select — retrieve only the documents, files, or tool outputs relevant to the current step (this is what RAG does for context)
Compress — periodically summarize older turns so history takes a fraction of the space
Isolate — hand sub-tasks to sub-agents with their own clean context, instead of growing one giant shared context
Cache — keep a stable prefix (system prompt, tool definitions) unchanged so it can be reused cheaply across turns
slides.body: Unlike prompt engineering (wording one request well), context engineering manages the whole pipeline feeding the model across a task.
slides.title: Four Levers of Context Engineering

bullets: Task arrives → retrieve only what's relevant (select) instead of preloading everything
Agent acts, generating tool calls and results → these accumulate in context
Periodically: summarize old turns into a compact running state (compress)
Large sub-problems get delegated to a fresh sub-agent context, with only the result returned to the parent (isolate)
Static scaffolding (system prompt, tool schemas) stays untouched at the front of the context (cache)
slides.title: Where It Fits in an Agent Loop

bullets: Naive approach: read every file it touches into context and never remove anything — by call 40, the context is dominated by stale file contents and the agent forgets the original bug report

Engineered approach: retrieve only the files relevant to the current hypothesis, summarize earlier exploration into a short scratchpad ('checked auth.py — not the issue'), and keep the original task description pinned at the top
Result: the agent stays focused on the actual bug dozens of steps later, instead of drifting
slides.body: An agent is asked to fix a bug across a 500-file codebase.
slides.title: A Coding Agent on a Large Repo

rows: Stays consistent — key facts stay near the top

slides.title: Naive Context vs. Engineered Context

bullets: Over-aggressive summarization can silently drop a detail the agent needed later — compaction is lossy by nature
Isolating too many sub-agents adds coordination overhead and can lose shared context a task actually needed
There's no universal policy — what to keep, compress, or drop is task-specific and needs real evaluation, not guesswork
For short, single-turn prompts, this overhead usually isn't worth it — context engineering pays off on long-horizon, multi-step tasks
slides.title: Where It Goes Wrong

bullets: Context engineering manages what fills the window across a whole task, not just how one prompt reads
The four core levers: select (retrieve), compress (summarize), isolate (sub-agents), cache (stable prefixes)
Models lose reliability on information buried mid-context — keep critical facts near the start or end
It's a tradeoff discipline: compaction risks losing detail, isolation risks losing shared context — tune per task
slides.title: Key Takeaways

questions.explanation: Prompt engineering optimizes a single request's wording. Context engineering is the broader, ongoing task of deciding what information populates the model's context across an entire agent run.
questions.prompt: How does context engineering differ from prompt engineering?
options: They are the same thing with different names
Context engineering manages everything that fills the context window across a multi-step task, not just the wording of one prompt
Context engineering only applies to image models
Prompt engineering is a subset of context engineering that only RAG systems use

questions.explanation: Isolation keeps a sub-task's exploration (file reads, intermediate reasoning) out of the main agent's context by handing it to a sub-agent, which reports back only a condensed result.
questions.prompt: What does 'isolate' mean as a context engineering lever?
options: Blocking the model from using any tools
Delegating a sub-task to a sub-agent with its own separate context, returning only the result to the parent
Running the model with no system prompt
Preventing the model from retrieving any documents

questions.explanation: Compaction trades completeness for space. If it discards something that mattered later in the task, the agent can make a mistake with no obvious cause — a core tradeoff to watch for.
questions.prompt: What's a real risk of over-aggressive context compaction (summarization)?
options: It makes the model respond faster than the hardware allows
It can silently drop a detail the agent still needed, since summarization is inherently lossy
It always doubles the token cost of a task
It is not possible to summarize tool outputs
